description:
High school student from Uralsk on the Field Shift challenge. I'm building a low-cost Arduino station that measures soil moisture in the steppe and combines it with NASA SMAP & POWER data to help West Kazakhstan farmers adapt to drought. I bring hardware and real ground data. Looking for: Python coding, data analysis, web dev. Join to build something real!
Ищу программистов и тех, кто работает с данными.
summary:
SteppeTruth helps farmers in West Kazakhstan choose what to sow for the next three years so their fields don’t run dry. The region gets only 190–320 mm of rain a year, and grain yields swing more than twofold between drought years and good years. A rotation is planned three years ahead, so one wrong choice in a dry year can cost a whole harvest.

We built a low-cost Arduino soil sensor (moisture and temperature), tested it in air, water, and dry and wet soil, and a bilingual website that pulls 45 years of NASA POWER data for Uralsk: rainfall and surface and root-zone soil wetness. The site compares current soil moisture with the long-term norm, sets our sensor readings beside NASA’s, and ranks three-year rotations of 10 crops plus fallow for dry, median and wet years by the farmer’s priority: water, soil or income. Every recommendation explains why and names its risks.

Next steps: NASA SMAP integration, field calibration of the sensor, and review of the rules by local agronomists.
details:
What it does and how it works

SteppeTruth helps farmers in West Kazakhstan decide what to sow over the next three years so their fields don’t run dry. The region receives only 190–320 mm of rain a year, and grain yields can differ more than twofold between a drought year (8.7 c/ha in 2018) and a good year (21 c/ha reported in 2026). Because rotations are planned three years ahead, one wrong choice in a dry year can cost a harvest.

The project has three parts:

  1. Ground sensor. An Arduino Uno with a capacitive soil moisture sensor and a DS18B20 temperature probe takes a reading every 10 seconds. We calibrated it in air (460), water (202), dry soil (~294) and wet soil (~204), so it clearly tells dry soil from wet.
  2. NASA data. Our website pulls NASA POWER data for Uralsk directly in the browser: 45 years (1981–2025) of monthly rainfall and root-zone soil wetness, plus the last 120 days of daily surface and root-zone wetness. It classifies every year as dry, median or wet, and compares current soil moisture with the 45-year norm for the same month.
  3. Rotation advisor. The advisor evaluates 900 three-year rotations built from 10 crops suited to the dry steppe (winter and spring wheat, barley, millet, chickpea, pea, sunflower, safflower, oilseed flax, Sudan grass) plus bare fallow. Each rotation is scored on water, soil health and income for the expected type of year, the soil moisture at sowing and the farmer’s priority. The tool shows the three best options and a score for the farmer’s current rotation. Every recommendation explains why it was chosen and names its risks, such as cereals after cereals or deep-rooted crops drying the soil.

Benefits and expected impact

Farmers get a transparent, data-based answer to “what should I sow?”, given as a range for dry, median and wet years rather than a single forecast. That helps them lower the risk of crop failure in drought years, protect soil with legumes and diverse rotations, and plan income. The approach scales: for another region only the crop table and the rules change, while the NASA data stays the same.

Tools and technologies

  • Hardware: Arduino Uno, capacitive soil moisture sensor v1.2, DS18B20 waterproof temperature sensor, breadboard
  • Firmware: Arduino IDE (C++), OneWire and DallasTemperature libraries
  • Website: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with hand-built SVG charts, bilingual (Russian and English), hosted on GitHub Pages
  • Data: NASA POWER API (PRECTOTCORR, GWETROOT, GWETTOP); NASA SMAP L4 is planned
  • Presentation: Canva

Creativity

SteppeTruth joins a $10 field sensor with satellite-era NASA data so that each checks the other: the sensor knows one field precisely, NASA sees the whole region and 45 years of history. Instead of a black-box prediction, it gives explainable advice with stated risks and confidence. We also interviewed a local farmer to test the idea against real experience.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty and explainability: we show what we don’t know yet, and the farmer always makes the final decision.
  • Scale mismatch: a sensor measures centimetres, while NASA POWER covers a grid cell of tens of kilometres, so we present them side by side rather than as the same number.
  • Accessibility: free, no login, works on a phone, in two languages.
  • Current limitations: the sensor has been tested indoors and not yet calibrated in a field, SMAP integration needs an Earthdata account, and the scoring rules are qualitative and must be reviewed by local agronomists. Prices and pests are not modelled yet.
